\chapter{A Meal}
\label{ch:te-a-meal}
\hlchaptermodality{40}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say I am having a meal in Telugu, using the word an earlier chapter already used and never explained.}

Say \te{భోజనం} \te{చేద్దాం}, explain \te{భోజనం} against everyday \te{తిండి} the way Chapter 32 first set them side by side, and apologise for a late meal with Chapter 9's \te{క్షమించండి}.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[bhōjanaṁ]{\te{భోజనం} (bhōjanaṁ) — \textquotedblleft{}a meal,\textquotedblright{} a word this book named before it ever taught it}

\label{lesson:TE-C40-bhojanam}



\begin{quote}
Tea, then milk. This chapter's last word is not a drink — it is the meal you would sit down to with both.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{భోజనం}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\te{భోజనం}} — \emph{bhōjanaṁ} — \textbf{a meal}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\te{భోజనం} \te{చేద్దాం}.} — \emph{bhōjanaṁ cēddāṁ.} — \textquotedblleft{}Let's eat\textquotedblright{} (literally, \textquotedblleft{}let's do a meal\textquotedblright{}).
\end{quote}

The \emph{tinu} lesson already used this exact word, in passing, as the polite counterpart of native \textbf{\te{తిండి}} — without ever teaching it properly. This lesson finally does.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\te{భోజనం}} is Sanskrit \textbf{\dv{भोजन}}, built on \textbf{\dv{भुज्}} (\emph{bhuj}), \textquotedblleft{}to enjoy, to partake of, to eat.\textquotedblright{} It sits above native \textbf{\te{తిండి}} the same way \textbf{\te{దయచేసి}} sits above the everyday \textbf{-\te{అండి}} ending: a formal Sanskrit layer over a plain Dravidian floor. \textbf{\te{కన్ను}}, \textquotedblleft{}eye,\textquotedblright{} was a word this book had already used once, unglossed, inside an etymology note — this lesson does the very same thing for \textbf{\te{భోజనం}}, which was named earlier without ever being taught.

If a meal runs late, Telugu reaches for the apology word taught earlier: \textbf{\te{భోజనం} \te{ఆలస్యం} \te{అయింది}, \te{క్షమించండి}} — \textquotedblleft{}the meal is late, sorry\textquotedblright{} — the same respectful \textbf{-\te{అండి}} ending that first met you on \textbf{\te{దయచేసి}}'s own everyday alternative.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}bhōjanaṁ cēddāṁ\textquotedblright{} — let's eat
  \item native, then borrowed — \textquotedblleft{}tiṇḍi … bhōjanaṁ\textquotedblright{}
  \item the apology — \textquotedblleft{}bhōjanaṁ ālasyaṁ ayindi, kṣamin̄caṇḍi\textquotedblright{}
  \item the chapter — \textquotedblleft{}ṭī … pālu … bhōjanaṁ\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}let's eat.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Bhōjanaṁ cēddāṁ}.) Which earlier lesson already used \emph{bhōjanaṁ}, without teaching it as its own word? (\textbf{The \emph{tinu} lesson.}) Apologise for a late meal, using the word you learned earlier. (\emph{Bhōjanaṁ ālasyaṁ ayindi, kṣamin̄caṇḍi}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(dialogue)]{The table words, second pass — and how to ask for them}

\label{lesson:TE-C40-second-pass-meal}



\begin{quote}
Three words, from memory and without the page: tea, milk, and the word for a meal.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: three words, three different journeys}
The three sit together on a table and came from three different places:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{where it came from} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\te{టీ}} \emph{ṭī} & borrowed, and by sea rather than by the overland road \\
\textbf{\te{పాలు}} \emph{pālu} & the family's own — the whole Dravidian group shares it \\
\textbf{\te{భోజనం}} \emph{bhōjanaṁ} & Sanskrit, and formal in tone because of it \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{\te{భోజనం}} is the one to weigh. It is not the everyday word for food; it is the polite noun for \textbf{a meal}, the sit-down kind, and its tone is the reason it belongs beside \emph{please} rather than beside a shopping list.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: two ways to put \textquotedblleft{}please\textquotedblright{} on a request}]
Asking for any of the three uses what \textbf{\te{దయచేసి}} and the \textbf{‑\te{ండి}} ending settled:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item The \textbf{‑\te{ండి}} ending on the verb is where ordinary Telugu keeps \emph{please}. A request with it is already polite.
  \item \textbf{\te{దయచేసి}} is the extra warmth on top — formal, or emphatic, and not the everyday word English speakers expect it to be.
\end{itemize}

So \textbf{\te{దయచేసి} \te{టీ}} is a warm, slightly formal ask, and the same request made with a ‑\te{ండి} verb and no \textbf{\te{దయచేసి}} is the ordinary polite one. Neither is rude.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn: ask for each}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item tea, please — the two-word form you learned with it
  \item the same ask with milk in place of tea
  \item the word for a meal, and notice it sounds more formal than the other two
  \item which of the three a host would offer you first
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of the three words is the family's own? (\textbf{\te{పాలు}}.) Which arrived from Sanskrit, and what does that do to its tone? (\textbf{\te{భోజనం}} — it makes it \textbf{formal}.) Where does everyday Telugu keep \emph{please}? (\textbf{In the ‑\te{ండి} ending on the verb.}) And what is \textbf{\te{దయచేసి}} for? (\textbf{Extra warmth, or formality, on top of an ending that is already polite.})
\end{tcolorbox}
